title: Can I castle right now?
outcomes: Goes through the castling conditions in order and names the one that stops castling
Knows an attacked rook, or an attacked b-square, does not stop castling
Looks only at the squares the king crosses and lands on for attacks

steps.text: In **Castling, and when you cannot** you met the conditions. Use them as a checklist in this order: has the king or that rook moved (the right is gone for good)? Is any piece between them? Is the king in check now? Is a square the king crosses or lands on attacked? As a **rule of thumb**, go from the cheapest question to the dearest and stop at the first no.

steps.caption: A black rook attacks b1, yet White can castle queenside: the king uses only e1, d1 and c1.

line.say: The king goes to c1 and the rook to d1, although b1 is attacked.

steps.text: Only the king's own path matters. Kingside that is e1, f1, g1; queenside it is e1, d1, c1. An attacked **rook** does not stop castling, and neither does an attacked square beside the queenside rook (b1). But an attacked f1 or d1 does, even if the king would land on a safe square. A lost right never comes back, even if the piece returns.

steps.title: A rook is attacked, then a path square, then nothing relevant
steps.prompt: Black's rook can stand on h8 or f8, or a knight can stand on a8. Predict first: in which of the three can White castle kingside?
Before each answer, which question of the checklist did you ask first? Which one did you skip, and did skipping it ever give a wrong answer?
